# Compounding Pressures and Scaling Limits {#sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales}

::: {.epigraph}
> "[F]eedback is a method of controlling a system by reinserting into it the results of its past performance. If these results are merely used as numerical data for the criticism of the system and its regulation, we have the simple feedback of the control engineers."
>
> — Norbert Wiener, *The Human Use of Human Beings*, revised edition [@Wiener1989HumanUse, p. 61]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *Why has system and chip design become harder to carry through, and where might AI assistance be useful?*

**Core thesis:** *Compounding pressures across physical scaling, specialization, software co-evolution, and verification demand new abstractions, but assistance helps only when it targets the work that actually limits the next design decision.*
:::

System and chip design increasingly depends on choices that must be evaluated together. Device scaling still improves transistor density, but no longer supplies the same broadly reusable gains in frequency and energy efficiency. Specialization, local data reuse, and new packaging can recover performance, while binding the result more tightly to software and physical implementation. Each promising architectural change can therefore require work in several disciplines before its value is known.

This chapter explains how those pressures increase the cost of obtaining useful answers. It follows the consequences of scaling limits through system composition and software change to the inputs, runtime, and verification needed to compare candidates. The resulting bottleneck differs across projects (@fig-ch02-cover-map). Identifying that limiting work is the first step toward judging whether point AI assistance, an AI-native design system, or conventional automation can improve the study; complexity alone establishes no need for AI.

![**Compounding pressures shift the architectural bottleneck.** Fading automatic technology gains, coupled design obligations across hardware and software, and finite simulation and verification capacity converge to limit design velocity. AI assistance helps most when it targets the specific engineering work delaying the next supported decision.](images/ch02-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch02-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Chapter overview diagram in which fading technology gains, coupled design obligations, and finite checking capacity converge on the work limiting the next supported decision."}

A team waiting for a compiler path faces a different problem from one waiting for simulations or expert review. The chapter's pressures provide ways to explain such delays, while measurements from the project determine which work must improve.

## Where Engineering Time Goes in Modern Chip Design

The cost of architectural exploration is visible in a familiar design choice. When an architect considers expanding an on-chip Level-2 (L2) cache to relieve memory bandwidth pressure, a capacity-focused simulation may favor the larger cache because it reduces misses. In silicon, however, the additional static random-access memory (SRAM) bitcells consume die area, lengthen interconnects,[^fn-rc-delay-c02] and increase leakage current. Within the thermal envelope of a passively cooled mobile device, that extra leakage reduces the power budget left for the compute cores, so a simulated drop in cache misses answers only part of the architectural question.

[^fn-rc-delay-c02]: **Interconnect resistance and capacitance**: A wire has electrical resistance, while neighboring conductors contribute capacitance. Charging that capacitance through the resistance takes time. Narrower wires increase resistance, and long connections add both resistance and capacitance, so a larger storage structure can take longer to access even when its transistors switch quickly.

Software offers another way to attack the same memory bottleneck. Loop tiling can reduce the working set that must remain on chip at one time, allowing a smaller cache or buffer to retain useful data, although the tiled loops can add control overhead. If the schedule uses direct memory access (DMA) to feed an explicitly managed local buffer or scratchpad, it also incurs transfer-descriptor and coordination costs. Weighing a larger L2 cache against a tiled software schedule requires both an executable schedule and characterized physical memory macros. The architect has to decide which hardware–software pairs are worth testing and which measurements will separate them.

Earlier jumps in abstraction kept this kind of design complexity manageable by hiding lower-level detail behind automated tools. Register-transfer level (RTL) descriptions let engineers specify synchronous circuit behavior without placing individual gates by hand.[^fn-rtl-c02] Logic synthesis and place-and-route tools then generated the gate-level layout. Formal equivalence checking established functional agreement between the RTL and its implementation under stated assumptions, while static timing analysis checked path delays against declared timing constraints. As @sec-moonshot showed, those abstractions succeeded because trustworthy verification tools checked the lower-level implementation automatically. Today's cross-layer, specialized architectures strain that model because hardware and software choices interact across the boundary, forcing many more coupled candidates through those slow implementation and signoff tools.

[^fn-rtl-c02]: **RTL as an architectural contract**: RTL specifies synchronous state updates and transfers between registers. Changing pipeline stages or interface timing can require restructuring these transfers, so an architectural alternative may need more implementation work than changing a parameter.

A *design path* is a sequence of work that proposes an architectural change, builds candidate artifacts, runs the relevant tools, and compares the results. In the cache study, one path evaluates two L2 capacities under a representative workload. It becomes a closed *design loop* only when returned evidence changes the represented design state and triggers another allowed action. High leakage might cause the architect to retain a smaller cache and evaluate a tiled schedule next. A fixed parameter sweep collects measurements across a preset grid; a design loop uses the results to determine subsequent work. This closing condition distinguishes a loop from a sequence of successful tool runs.

Every turn of that loop spends engineering time, electronic design automation (EDA) tool licenses, and human review on inputs that span RTL source, execution traces, timing constraints, and power-intent specifications. Depending on the project, the slowest step may be assembling those candidate files, waiting on physical signoff runs, or diagnosing verification failures. The breakdown of classical transistor and wire scaling explains why more architectural choices now require such cross-layer experiments.

## The End of Free Scaling and the Push Toward Specialization {#sec-fracturing-technology-dividend}

For roughly thirty years, processor performance advanced under classical Dennard scaling, where shrinking physical device dimensions reduced transistor area and gate delay while voltage scaling allowed more transistors to switch faster without increasing power density (@tbl-dennard-scaling-comparison) [@Moore1965Cramming; @DennardEtAl1974Scaling; @HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach]. Today, device technology still supplies transistor density, but it no longer delivers proportional gains in frequency, single-thread performance, or energy efficiency. To extract more performance, architects now have to make choices that tightly bind microarchitecture, software mapping, and physical implementation together.

### The Collapse of Dennard Scaling and the Shift to Specialization

Classical Dennard scaling balanced denser transistors against lower power per transistor. Shrinking linear dimensions by a factor $\kappa > 1$ reduced area by $1/\kappa^2$, while lower capacitance and supply voltage reduced switching energy enough to permit a higher clock frequency at constant dynamic power density [@DennardEtAl1974Scaling]. The dynamic-power relation $P_{\mathrm{dyn}} = \alpha C V_{dd}^{2} f$ makes voltage's role explicit: its contribution is squared, alongside switching activity $\alpha$, capacitance $C$, and frequency $f$.

The comparison in @tbl-dennard-scaling-comparison isolates what changes when voltage and frequency stop scaling. Its simplified post-Dennard case holds activity, voltage, and frequency fixed while retaining idealized area and gate-capacitance scaling. Leakage and interconnect capacitance are excluded from that calculation; real implementations require both.

| Device Parameter | Classical Dennard Scaling ($\kappa > 1$) | Simplified Post-Dennard Case | Limiting Physical Constraint |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Transistor Area ($W \times L$)** | $1/\kappa^2$ | $1/\kappa^2$ | Gate pitch scaling continues |
| **Supply Voltage ($V_{dd}$)** | $1/\kappa$ | $1$ *(held fixed)* | Leakage and switching-speed trade-off |
| **Gate Capacitance ($C_{\text{gate}}$)** | $1/\kappa$ | $1/\kappa$ *(idealized)* | Gate and interconnect capacitance scale differently |
| **Operating Frequency ($f$)** | $\kappa$ | $1$ *(held fixed)* | Thermal dissipation and leakage limit frequency gains |
| **Dynamic Power Density ($P_{\mathrm{dyn}} / A$)** | $1$ *(constant)* | $\kappa$ *(under stated assumptions)* | Dark silicon and thermal limits |
: **Classical Dennard scaling versus a simplified post-Dennard case.** Shrinking linear dimensions by a factor $\kappa > 1$ historically kept dynamic power density constant while increasing operating frequency. With voltage, frequency, and activity held fixed in the displayed post-Dennard case, dynamic power density rises by $\kappa$; leakage, interconnect, and nonideal geometric scaling make real product behavior implementation-dependent. {#tbl-dennard-scaling-comparison tbl-colwidths="[24,24,28,24]"}

Under the table's post-Dennard assumptions, power per transistor falls more slowly than transistor density rises. More transistors can therefore fit in the same area without all being able to switch at once within the same power budget. Leakage and interconnect costs further affect the usable fraction in a physical chip.

The classical balance broke down in the mid-2000s because supply voltage could no longer fall alongside feature size. Lower voltage slows transistor switching unless the threshold voltage also drops, but lowering that threshold increases off-state leakage. Device physics thus forces a trade-off among switching speed, active power, and leakage. Once voltage reductions stalled, process shrinks alone could no longer deliver simultaneous gains in clock frequency and energy efficiency [@HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach].

Fifty years of microprocessor scaling data from Karl Rupp's CPU sample (1971–2021), joined with a 2012–2026 frontier compiled from the published specifications of twenty-five accelerators including GPUs [@FoleyDanskin2017Pascal; @ChoquetteEtAl2018Volta; @JouppiEtAl2021TenLessons; @ChoquetteEtAl2021Ampere; @Choquette2023Hopper; @AMD2025CDNA3; @NVIDIA2024B100; @NVIDIA2013K20XBoardSpec; @AMD2021CDNA2; @Myrhang2023AMDInstinctHPC; @Intel2023Gaudi2Datasheet; @Intel2024Gaudi3Whitepaper; @NVIDIA2024BlackwellDatasheet; @NVIDIA2025BlackwellUltraBlog; @NVIDIA2026RubinBlog; @Cerebras2019WSE; @Cerebras2021WSE2; @Cerebras2024WSE3], map this architectural evolution across three eras (@fig-microprocessor-trends). In the *device-scaling era* (1971–2005), single-thread performance, clock frequency, and transistor counts all climbed by orders of magnitude, though at different rates. Around the 2005 Dennard boundary, clock frequency stalled near $3\text{--}5\ \text{GHz}$ in this sample, and single-thread performance growth fell from about 52% per year (1986–2003) to about 23% per year, dropping to single digits by the late 2010s [@HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach]. This slowdown ushered in the *parallelism era* (2005–2016), as architects turned to multicore integration and sampled hardware thread counts climbed to 96 by 2016 and 128 by 2020. Over that span, maximum reported CPU power in each four-year bucket rose from about $200\ \text{W}$ in the mid-2010s to about $290\ \text{W}$ by 2021 (where the CPU series ends, without establishing a power ceiling for later processors). A third inflection around 2016 marks the *specialization era*, as dedicated datapaths became an increasingly important use of growing transistor budgets.

<!-- arch2-allow: figure-placement-override The readable stacked plot was deferred several pages under top-only placement. -->
![**Frequency scaling slows as transistor budgets and accelerator power ratings grow.** Four-year maxima from Rupp's CPU sample (1971–2021) [@Rupp2022MicroprocessorTrendData] join running maxima from twenty-five accelerators (2012–2026). Accelerator counts reach 336 billion transistors (4 trillion for wafer-scale parts), and power ratings reach $1{,}400\ \text{W}$. Ratings mix thermal design power, board-power limits, and total graphics power, not measured workload power. The CPU series establishes no later power ceiling. Accelerator sources and six dated design reports appear in the text; the hatched band after 2026 marks the emerging AI-native design frontier rather than a fourth measured trend.](images/fig-microprocessor-trends){#fig-microprocessor-trends width="100%" fig-pos="!htbp" fig-alt="Log-scale chart with CPU sample maxima ending in 2021 and accelerator specification frontiers extending to 2026. CPU frequency growth slows after 2005, while transistor counts and accelerator power ratings increase. A hatched band after 2026 marks a hypothesized AI-native design era; a separate rail dates six AI-assisted design reports."}

The divergence of these curves after 2005 reflects the *dark silicon* limit [@Sutter2005FreeLunch; @EsmaeilzadehEtAl2011DarkSilicon].[^fn-dark-silicon-c02] Once supply voltage stopped scaling, thermal budgets capped the fraction of a chip's transistors that could switch simultaneously at full clock frequency. Duplicating general-purpose cores during the parallelism era converted extra transistors into thread-level concurrency, but serial code sections and shared-memory traffic soon limited the return on adding more homogeneous cores.

Specialization answers that limit by spending the transistor and power budget on dedicated datapaths. Packaged accelerator transistor counts climb from 15.3 billion in the NVIDIA Tesla P100 (2016) to 208 billion in the dual-die Blackwell B200 (2024) and 336 billion in NVIDIA's Rubin GPU (2026), while Cerebras integrates 4 trillion transistors on a single wafer-scale die. Over the same span, published accelerator power ratings rise from the P100's $300\ \text{W}$ thermal design power (TDP) to as much as $1{,}400\ \text{W}$ total graphics power in the Blackwell Ultra generation (2025). Although these ratings describe nominal hardware envelopes rather than measured application efficiency, they show why the industry has directed its silicon budget into regular matrix and tensor arrays that amortize instruction fetch and decode across hundreds of arithmetic units, trading clock-rate scaling for dense spatial parallelism and local data reuse.

The hatched band in @fig-microprocessor-trends identifies the design process as a possible next source of improvement, rather than a measured successor to specialization. The dated reports alongside it document early applications to placement, design support, circuits, and generated processors or accelerators [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement; @LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo; @Verkor2026DesignConductor; @Verkor2026DesignConductor2; @DeepMind2026AlphaEvolveImpact; @OpenAI2026JalapenoFirstResults]. They do not establish that an AI-native design system reduces total project cost against a comparably equipped conventional team. The pressure that motivates such a comparison begins with the increasing effort needed to exploit each additional transistor.

[^fn-dark-silicon-c02]: **Dark silicon**: Silicon that cannot all operate concurrently at full performance within the available power and thermal budget. Power gating, clock gating, and reduced operating rates are among the ways a design manages that limit.

### Diminishing Returns Inside General-Purpose Cores

General-purpose processors continue to improve through branch prediction, speculative execution, wider issue, and better memory hierarchies. These mechanisms can expose and exploit more instruction-level parallelism, but their benefits must pay for the structures needed to coordinate that work.

The out-of-order issue window illustrates that cost. More entries let a core look farther ahead for independent instructions, while wider issue allows more instructions to execute per cycle. Completing instructions must broadcast result tags to waiting entries, however, and selection logic must choose which ready instructions proceed. Enlarging the window increases the load on those broadcast wires; widening issue adds comparison, arbitration, and bypass paths. Circuit analysis shows how wakeup, selection, and bypass delays limit the return on wider issue [@PalacharlaEtAl1997ComplexityEffective], while wire delay restricts how far a signal can travel in a clock cycle [@AgarwalEtAl2000ClockRateVersusIPC].

Replicating cores shifts the cost toward coherence, synchronization, and workload partitioning. General-purpose architectures continue to advance, but useful parallelism has to pay for the structures that coordinate it. Regular workloads offer an alternative: dedicate more of the transistor budget to arithmetic and local storage, with less coordination per operation.

### The Shift to Domain-Specific Accelerators

When a workload performs regular, predictable calculations, a specialized datapath can strip away most of that per-instruction coordination hardware and devote the silicon to dense arithmetic arrays, provided the memory system can keep those units fed.

Across five NVIDIA GPU generations from Pascal P100 (2016) to Blackwell B200 (2024), peak dense half-precision floating-point (FP16) throughput grew by $106\times$ ($21.2\text{ to }2{,}250\ \text{TFLOPS}$), outpacing the $10.9\times$ growth in off-chip High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) supply ($732\text{ to }8{,}000\ \text{GB/s}$) by roughly an order of magnitude while TDP rose $3.3\times$ ($300\text{ to }1{,}000\ \text{W}$) (@fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier a). With precision held fixed and excluding structured sparsity,[^fn-structured-sparsity-c02] this divergence reflects an architectural pivot from P100's conventional vector units to dedicated matrix Tensor Cores across successive process nodes and dual-reticle packaging [@FoleyDanskin2017Pascal; @ChoquetteEtAl2018Volta; @ChoquetteEtAl2021Ampere; @Choquette2023Hopper; @NVIDIA2024BlackwellTechBrief].

[^fn-structured-sparsity-c02]: **Structured sparsity**: Sparse matrices contain zero values whose arithmetic can sometimes be skipped. Hardware-supported structured sparsity limits the patterns of nonzero values so that dedicated hardware can process the remaining values efficiently. Advertised sparse throughput assumes those patterns; the comparison here uses dense throughput throughout.

Because arithmetic capacity expanded far faster than off-chip memory bandwidth, feeding these datapaths demands much higher data reuse inside the package. If we define a workload's *operational intensity* as the arithmetic operations executed per byte transferred across the HBM boundary, dividing peak compute rate by memory bandwidth gives the off-chip balance point plotted in @fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier b [@Williams2009Roofline]. That dense FP16 balance point escalates tenfold from $29\ \text{FLOP/byte}$ on P100 to $295\ \text{FLOP/byte}$ on H100, before plateauing at $281\ \text{FLOP/byte}$ on B200 as eight-stack HBM3e bandwidth ($8\ \text{TB/s}$) keeps pace with the $2.3\times$ step in dense FP16 compute (while B200's narrower 8-bit and 4-bit floating-point [FP8 and FP4] Tensor Core modes push the required reuse another $2\times\text{ to }4\times$ higher). A kernel operating below its target precision's balance point cannot saturate the matrix engines even with zero control stalls. Greater on-chip data reuse raises the kernel's operational intensity by reducing HBM traffic, whereas more HBM bandwidth lowers the hardware's balance point at a fixed peak compute rate.

![**Arithmetic scaling outpaces off-chip memory bandwidth.** (a) Growth relative to P100 in dense FP16 peak throughput, HBM bandwidth, and TDP across five GPU generations from P100 to B200 (2016–2024). (b) The dense FP16 off-chip balance point rises from 29\ FLOP/byte on P100 to 295\ FLOP/byte on H100 and 281\ FLOP/byte on B200, demanding steep operational intensity to saturate peak arithmetic. Hardware specifications exclude structured sparsity [@FoleyDanskin2017Pascal; @NVIDIA2016P100Datasheet; @ChoquetteEtAl2018Volta; @ChoquetteEtAl2021Ampere; @Choquette2023Hopper; @NVIDIA2022H100Whitepaper; @NVIDIA2024BlackwellTechBrief; @NVIDIA2024BlackwellDatasheet].](images/fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier){#fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier width="100%" fig-alt="Two-panel chart for P100, V100, A100, H100, and B200 GPUs from 2016 to 2024. First panel shows dense FP16 peak throughput growing 106 times relative to P100 while HBM bandwidth grows 10.9 times and TDP grows 3.3 times. Second panel shows the dense FP16 off-chip balance point rising from 29 floating-point operations per byte transferred from HBM on P100 to 295 on H100 and 281 on B200."}

### Why Accelerators Coupled the Hardware and Software Stacks

This divergence between arithmetic density and memory supply erodes the classical separation of concerns inside an accelerator design. Where a conventional processor stack lets compiler writers, microarchitects, and process engineers work against relatively independent interfaces, @fig-tao-vs-taos contrasts that modular hierarchy with the coupled regime of domain-specific hardware, in which a single power, thermal, and area envelope ties all three layers together.

![**Specialization makes cross-layer dependencies explicit.** (a) A classical layered view separates optimization, architecture, and technology into modular tiers. (b) The specialization-coupled view reveals how domain specialization binds software mapping, microarchitecture, and silicon fabrication across shared power, thermal, and area constraints.](images/fig-tao-vs-taos){#fig-tao-vs-taos width="80%" fig-alt="Two side-by-side stack diagrams. The first panel shows optimization, architecture, and technology stacked in a top-down hierarchy. The second panel introduces a specialization block coupled across all three tiers, bounded by a shared thermal, power, and area constraint perimeter."}

Specialization does not invent cross-layer coupling, but it removes the slack that once hid it. When an architect chooses a systolic or tensor-core array geometry, that choice fixes which dataflows keep operands local; sizing the on-chip scratchpad to sustain that reuse dictates die area and wire reach; and those physical layout choices determine clock frequency and leakage in the chosen process node. An architectural model that evaluates datapath throughput without accounting for on-chip storage area and physical wire delay can misrank candidates inside the block. Even when a block's internal datapath, storage, and wires are well balanced, however, its value still depends on how it fits into the surrounding system.

```{=latex}
\FloatBarrier
```

## Balancing Specialization and System Composition

A specialized engine delivers a system speedup only when the surrounding machine can supply its inputs and use its outputs. The host still executes control flow, the runtime moves data and synchronizes execution, and shared memories and links serve other clients. The architect must therefore compare complete organizations, including the software and communication needed to use each block, before deciding which specialized capability is worth its area and power.

### From Kernel Efficiency to System Speedup

Specialization can produce large local gains by removing general-purpose machinery. For the H.264 video encoder studied by @HameedEtAl2010Inefficiency, a fixed-function application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) improved kernel energy efficiency roughly 500-fold relative to a four-core chip multiprocessor by eliminating instruction fetch and decode overhead and fusing operator pipelines. That result explains the attraction of specialization, but the fraction of the application accelerated and the cost of reaching the block determine how much benefit survives in a full system.

Amdahl's law makes this distinction explicit. If a fraction $f$ of baseline execution receives a local speedup $S_{\mathrm{accel}}$, the total speedup including communication is

$$S_{\mathrm{total}} = \frac{1}{(1-f) + \frac{f}{S_{\mathrm{accel}}} + t_{\mathrm{comm}}}$${#eq-amdahl-communication}

where $t_{\mathrm{comm}}$ is the added, nonoverlapped transfer and synchronization time normalized to baseline execution time. Even with free communication, an infinitely fast accelerator cannot exceed $1/(1-f)$ total speedup [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor]. The unaccelerated host work in @eq-amdahl-communication remains, and communication lowers the ceiling further.

How strongly this bound limits a design depends on the workload. Under Gustafson's law, a system can increase its parallel work as more processors become available, as a training study might do with a larger model or dataset [@Gustafson1988AmdahlLaw]. A latency-critical mobile extended-reality (XR) pipeline instead has fixed per-frame work and a deadline. Dispatch and synchronization consume time that extra arithmetic units cannot recover.

The LogCA accelerator model separates the costs hidden inside the communication term [@AltafWood2017LogCA]. The useful distinction here is between a fixed cost paid for each invocation and a data-transfer cost that grows with the work. For a simple offload with no overlap, completion time is the sum of invocation time, accelerator execution time, and transfer time. Offloading helps only when that sum is smaller than execution on an optimized host.

Consider a neural processing unit (NPU) invoked separately for each small layer of a neural network. Command preparation, queue submission, and synchronization can consume much of the elapsed time even when the matrix arithmetic finishes quickly. Fusing layers or batching requests places more useful work behind each launch and can move the workload beyond its break-even payload size. But batching alone cannot remove a transfer cost that grows in proportion to the arithmetic. If moving each additional operation's data takes at least as much time as offloading saves on that operation, no larger payload makes the nonoverlapped offload profitable. The design needs fewer transferred bytes, more link bandwidth, or effective overlap.

These remedies cross different boundaries. A compiler may retain intermediate tensors on chip and reduce traffic without changing the interface. A lower-cost submission path changes how the runtime invokes the accelerator, while a wider physical link changes the hardware. The actual launch path, achieved bandwidth, data reuse, and host baseline determine which remedy helps; a link specification alone cannot settle the comparison. An empirical sweep across payload sizes tests where, if anywhere, the complete offload becomes faster than host execution.

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="The unamortized offload wall"}
**The trap.** A team treats the local matrix-multiply acceleration of an NPU as the expected system speedup.

**The mechanism.** Small layers may contain too little work to amortize each invocation, while input and output transfers add costs that grow with the workload. An optimized host can also erase an apparent gain measured against scalar code.

**The lesson.** Compare complete offloads against optimized host execution. Test whether fusion, batching, local reuse, or a cheaper submission path changes the result. If feasible changes still leave the offload below break-even, retaining host execution is the supported choice.
:::

The offload comparison thus requires more than a faster datapath. It needs a workable mapping and invocation path, and it may require changing the boundary between software and hardware. Integrating the resulting blocks adds a further set of physical and behavioral constraints.

### Packaging and Wafer-Scale Communication {#sec-wafer-scale-communication-tradeoffs}

Partitioning a large design into chiplets can improve manufacturing yield under random-defect models, let different functions use separate process nodes, and spread development cost across products. Those benefits must pay for packaging, test, assembly losses, and die-to-die communication [@Murphy1964CostSize; @FengMa2022ChipletActuary]. A partition that looks favorable in a block diagram may require more bandwidth than the available die edge can carry. The bandwidth available per unit of edge, or *shoreline bandwidth density*, depends on interface placement, connection pitch, and signaling rate, so the partition and the package have to be evaluated together.

Standard interfaces reduce part of the integration burden. Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) specifies die-to-die physical layers and protocols [@UCIeConsortium2026Spec], while pre-bond testing helps screen defective chiplets before an expensive assembly step [@IEEE2020Std1838]. Neither establishes that the finished system has enough power, cooling, or bandwidth. Known-good-die testing also leaves the possibility of test escapes and assembly failures.

Keeping compute and storage on a wafer changes these trade-offs rather than removing them. The Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine keeps communication on a large compute and SRAM fabric [@Cerebras2019WSE], reducing reliance on board-level links while requiring specialized power delivery, cooling, and defect tolerance. In a wafer-scale GPU case study, physical constraints reduced usable capacity from a nominal 100 GPU modules to 40 [@PalEtAl2019WaferscaleGPU]. Available silicon area therefore does not directly determine usable compute; placement, defect routing, and software scheduling determine which resources a workload can exploit.

Composition also creates failures that do not appear when blocks are checked separately. Third-party intellectual property (IP) delivered as fixed hard macros or encrypted RTL restricts integration teams to documented behavior, supplied models, and accessible interfaces [@Arm2013CortexA15HardMacro; @Intel2024EncryptedRTLIP]. Even when blocks implement a standard bus [@Arm2020AXI], incompatible reset, power-sequencing, or clock-domain assumptions can prevent them from operating together. The Semiconductor Research Corporation (SRC) Microelectronics and Advanced Packaging Technologies (MAPT) roadmap identifies inconsistent supplier data formats and semantics as an obstacle to cross-vendor automation [@SemiconductorResearchCorporation2023MAPT]. A search cannot safely treat missing compatibility information as permission to combine blocks, and obtaining that information consumes engineering time before performance evaluation can begin.

### Choosing the System Boundary

The same composition problem extends beyond a package. A candidate accelerator may finish its own kernel sooner yet send enough extra traffic across a shared fabric to delay the end-to-end request. Whenever an interaction can reverse which design wins, the evaluation boundary must include it. The progression from cores to warehouse-scale systems in @fig-architecture-levers identifies the additional obligations that arise as that boundary expands.

<!-- arch2-allow: figure-placement-override The tall print-size scale diagram needs a full-page float option near its discussion. -->
![**The study boundary must include interactions that can change the decision.** Stacked from warehouse-scale deployment at the top down to core execution at the bottom, five compute scales illustrate how comparison obligations funnel outward as the system boundary expands upward from a core. A broader study may reuse component models; it need not reproduce every lower-level detail at the same fidelity.](images/fig-architecture-levers){#fig-architecture-levers width="100%" fig-pos="!htbp" fig-alt="Diagram of five architecture scales stacked from warehouse-scale system at the top down through wafer-scale system, system-on-chip or chiplet, accelerator, and core at the bottom, funneling outward as the system boundary expands upward from core to warehouse-scale. Each scale adds named obligations to a common comparison path feeding one cross-scale architecture comparison."}

At warehouse scale, placement and sharing decisions couple servers, networks, distributed runtimes, cooling, and facility power [@BarrosoHolzleRanganathan2019DatacenterAsComputer]. Within and across nodes, cache-coherent interconnects such as Compute Express Link (CXL) make pooled memory another architectural choice [@CXLConsortium2026CXL]. These mechanisms belong inside the study when they can change its target metric, whether tail latency, sustained throughput, or total cost.

A broader boundary does not require cycle-level simulation of every component. Architects combine characterized component models with trace-driven or discrete-event simulation, hardware testbeds, and production telemetry. The combination must preserve the relevant interactions: independent trace replays can miss shared-network contention, while mean response times hide stragglers that govern tail latency at scale [@DeanBarroso2013TailAtScale]. Choosing the smallest boundary that captures effects capable of reversing the decision limits evaluation cost without assuming those effects away.

Within that boundary, a hardware organization still needs software that can use it. The offload example shows why compiler mappings and runtime behavior belong in the comparison, and why changing either can alter the value of hardware that is already fixed.

## Workload Volatility and Software–Hardware Coupling

Hardware cannot realize a proposed gain without software that exercises the mechanism. A compiler can fuse operations into a payload large enough to amortize an accelerator launch, or introduce spills that erase the expected saving. The evaluation therefore needs an executable path to compile, schedule, and drive the candidate hardware. That path continues to change after silicon is fixed, creating two related pressures: making a specialized mechanism usable and keeping it useful as workloads evolve.

### Why Hardware Gains Require a Working Compiler Path

A custom matrix unit or instruction extension can excel in a hand-coded microbenchmark yet remain idle in an application if no compiler pass, kernel library, or runtime can use it effectively. An *executable software path* connects the programming model through compilation and libraries to the runtime, driver or firmware, and deployment controls. Different systems require different components, but the path must be complete enough to run the intended workload without losing the hardware benefit to extra transfers, spills, or dispatch overhead.

A *compiler narrow waist* shares part of this work through an intermediate representation (IR). Common transformations operate on the IR, while target-specific lowering maps operations onto a particular machine. Halide separates an algorithm from its execution schedule [@RaganKelleyEtAl2017HalideCACM]; Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) supports transformations across levels of abstraction [@LattnerEtAl2020MLIR]. These abstractions reduce duplication, but every target still needs lowering, runtime support, and validation suited to its hardware.

The path in @fig-codegen-narrow-waist locates that shared representation between source programs and target execution. A matrix instruction needs a lowering path that matches its operand layout; an asynchronous transfer engine needs scheduling and synchronization that preserve correctness. Those obligations connect compiler work directly to whether an architectural candidate can be evaluated at all.

![**Executable target software paths connect developer intent to verification checks.** High-level domain-specific abstract syntax trees (Python, Triton domain-specific languages) lower through mid-level control-data flow graphs in MLIR dialects and LLVM IR at the compiler narrow waist, where workload intent, architectural mechanisms such as CPU instruction-set extensions and NPU dataflows, and silicon constraints converge. Lowered machine code and runtimes then pass through verification checks for correctness, performance, portability, and maintainability.](images/fig-codegen-narrow-waist){#fig-codegen-narrow-waist width="80%" fig-alt="Diagram of an executable target software path showing programming models, compiler representations, libraries, runtimes, and generated code connecting hardware constraints to correctness, performance, portability, and maintainability checks."}

Once code reaches the target, its mapping can determine whether the offload pays. Fusing operations places more work behind each invocation, while retaining intermediate tensors on chip reduces traffic. These changes address the two distinct costs identified by LogCA. Yet fusion also keeps more values live at once, increasing register pressure. If those values exceed the available registers, the compiler spills them to memory and can undo the locality gain.

The RISC-V Vector extension makes the trade-off concrete. A compiler can group architectural vector registers to process more elements per instruction, but wider groups leave fewer independent groups for other live values [@RISCV2026UnprivilegedISA]. A fused kernel may therefore benefit from wide grouping until register spills add enough traffic to slow it down. Peak vector width cannot determine the winner; compiled execution with the intended data types and workload can.

An autotuner such as AutoTVM searches compiler schedules on a fixed machine [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM]. A joint hardware–software study varies the machine as well, so each hardware–schedule pair needs a fair evaluation. Holding one candidate's schedule fixed while tuning another can mistake software effort for architectural merit. Producing and checking the executable paths is thus part of the cost of comparing hardware alternatives, rather than a step that follows the architecture decision.

### Changing Software and Fixed Hardware {#sec-software-changes-faster-than-silicon}

An architectural comparison may become outdated while a chip is still being specified, verified, and fabricated. A memory hierarchy tuned for one model family and compiler release can encounter different tensor shapes, kernel schedules, and serving regimes at deployment. Before tapeout, hardware and software teams can revise the design together, although late hardware changes become expensive. After tapeout, software has to adapt the fixed machine.

Numerical formats make this commitment especially clear. Supporting FP8, 4-bit integer, or block-scale representations changes the arithmetic units and datapaths built into silicon. Block-scale formats share exponent or scale metadata across groups of elements [@RouhaniEtAl2023Microscaling], so their efficiency depends on a specific organization of values and metadata. A model that adopts a different format after the datapath is frozen may no longer use the hardware as efficiently. The architect must decide which workload properties are stable enough to specialize and where programmability is worth its area and energy cost.

Memory behavior can change just as sharply. Convolutional inference with fixed frame sizes follows a relatively regular schedule, whereas autoregressive Transformer serving retains a growing key-value (KV) cache of attention keys and values from earlier tokens to avoid recomputing them [@KwonEtAl2023PagedAttention]. Variable sequence lengths change the amount of stored state. Mixture-of-experts models route inputs to selected expert subnetworks [@ShazeerEtAl2017MoE], making traffic depend on the input, while prompt processing and incremental token generation form distinct prefill and decode phases [@AgrawalEtAl2024SarathiServe]. These changes alter how computation and memory traffic arrive. A larger working set can overflow a scratchpad and force transfers to dynamic random-access memory (DRAM); a smaller serving batch can leave too little work to amortize each accelerator invocation. The relevant question is which assumption changed and whether the hardware retains enough flexibility to accommodate it.

Deployment requirements can also change delivered throughput without changing the arithmetic or hardware. The matched MLPerf submissions below isolate one such pressure by comparing standard and interactive latency requirements on the same systems.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import json as _json2ml
from pathlib import Path as _Path2ml
import _python.plots as _ap2ml

_ml12 = _json2ml.loads(
    (_Path2ml(_ap2ml.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
     / "data" / "studies" / "12-mlperf-latency-contract" / "summary.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
)
ml12_pairs = _ml12["pairs"]
ml12_std_ttft = f"{round(_ml12['latency_contract_ms']['standard_ttft_ms']):,}"
ml12_std_tpot = f"{round(_ml12['latency_contract_ms']['standard_tpot_ms']):,}"
ml12_int_ttft = f"{round(_ml12['latency_contract_ms']['interactive_ttft_ms']):,}"
ml12_int_tpot = f"{round(_ml12['latency_contract_ms']['interactive_tpot_ms']):,}"
ml12_min_pct = f"{100 * _ml12['minimum_interactive_fraction']:.1f}"
ml12_max_pct = f"{100 * _ml12['maximum_interactive_fraction']:.1f}"
ml12_med_pct = f"{100 * _ml12['median_interactive_fraction']:.1f}"
```

Across `{python} ml12_pairs` matched single-node, eight-accelerator Llama 2 70B server submissions in MLPerf Inference v5.0 [@MLCommons2025InferenceV50Results], tightening 99th-percentile latency bounds from `{python} ml12_std_ttft`\ ms time to first token and `{python} ml12_std_tpot`\ ms time per output token (Standard) to `{python} ml12_int_ttft`\ ms and `{python} ml12_int_tpot`\ ms (Interactive) restricts interactive server throughput to `{python} ml12_min_pct`% to `{python} ml12_max_pct`% of standard throughput (median `{python} ml12_med_pct`%). The hardware has not changed, but the acceptable service behavior has. A throughput result established under the looser requirement cannot answer the stricter design question.

This distinction also separates a better implementation from a different task. A faster kernel for the original workload can strengthen the case for existing hardware; a new model shape, accuracy target, or latency requirement changes what the machine must accomplish. Standardized benchmarks hold tasks and run rules fixed long enough to compare systems. Within a single MLPerf version, division, scenario, and accuracy target, teams can optimize their software while retaining a defined comparison [@ReddiEtAl2020MLPerfInference]. Once those conditions change, earlier measurements may need to be repeated.

Even a label such as mobile XR leaves much unspecified. Sensor fusion, head tracking, and neural rendering impose different deadlines and memory-access patterns across a system-on-chip (SoC). An XRBench workload [@KwonEtAl2023XRBench] still needs exact traces, model versions, and quality targets before it can distinguish candidate hardware. Fixing those inputs makes a comparison meaningful, but the hardware parameters and software mappings within it can still produce far more alternatives than the team can evaluate in detail.

## Why Coupled Design Spaces Outgrow Manual Search {#sec-evaluation-capacity-bounds-search}

Hardware parameters, dataflow mappings, and compiler schedules multiply the number of candidate designs within a study. That count alone says little about the work required to compare them. An analytical model may score a large space cheaply, while a much smaller set of candidates can consume the available budget if each requires detailed simulation, physical implementation, and new verification work.

Timeloop, an analytical framework for mapping and evaluating deep neural network (DNN) accelerators, illustrates the combinatorial growth [@ParasharEtAl2019Timeloop]. A convolutional layer has loops over batches, channels, output positions, and kernel positions. Each memory level introduces choices about how to order and divide those loops and which tensors to retain. A change in buffer capacity can make one mapping legal and another impossible, so the best mapping depends on the hardware being evaluated. The architect is searching coupled hardware and software choices even for one layer.

Practical exploration therefore eliminates illegal configurations, screens survivors with inexpensive models, and develops selected candidates far enough to run stronger checks. The published tasks in @tbl-design-loop-scale-anchors illustrate different costs along that path. Mapping and compiler tuning create many alternatives within a fixed machine; accelerator design-space exploration (DSE) and floorplanning also change the implementation that later checks must assess.

| **Architecture task** | **Scale anchor** | **Why candidate count is not enough** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| DNN accelerator mapping | Timeloop enumerates loop permutations, factorization choices, and level-bypass alternatives [@ParasharEtAl2019Timeloop]. | Mapping is itself a combinatorial problem; architecture evaluation depends on the mapper and its constraints. |
| DNN accelerator DSE | MAESTRO, an analytical cost model for estimating DNN dataflow performance, reports 480M candidates, 2.5M valid designs, and 0.17M designs/s [@KwonEtAl2019MAESTRO]. | Pruning rules determine which candidates are evaluated and which are never seen. |
| Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) block floorplanning | AlphaChip uses reinforcement learning to generate macro placements [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement]. | Reported gains depend on the cases, baselines, compute budgets, and downstream checks, which remain disputed in the reproduction, the reply, and the updated assessment [@ChengEtAl2023MacroPlacement; @GoldieEtAl2024ThatChipHasSailed; @ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment]. |
| Tensor-program tuning | AutoTVM, a machine learning-based tensor program optimizer, describes tensor-operator search spaces on the order of billions of possible implementations for a single GPU operator [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM]. | Compiler schedules create a hardware-dependent search problem of their own. |
: **Large search spaces place different demands on evaluation.** Mapping, accelerator DSE, floorplanning, and tensor-program tuning combine candidate scale, validity constraints, feedback cost, and different evidence requirements. {#tbl-design-loop-scale-anchors tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

\FloatBarrier

The MAESTRO result illustrates why a large count does not establish a need for a learned search method. Its analytical model evaluates dataflow choices quickly, although its rankings still depend on the workload and the physical effects represented by the model. Macro placement presents a different limitation: proposing coordinates does not establish that the resulting floorplan can be routed or meet timing. Both studies need selection, but they spend their evaluation budgets on different uncertainties.

The useful question is therefore how much work a candidate requires before it can inform a decision. Fast screening may make a broad search affordable, yet it cannot supply every fact about the finalists. Physical layout, realistic workload execution, and functional verification expose different reasons why a promising candidate may fail.

## Why Physical Layout, Simulation, and Verification Slow the Loop {#sec-stronger-evaluation-expensive}

A team can accelerate performance screening only to watch its preferred candidates fail timing closure or require more verification than the project can support. Physical implementation, workload simulation, and functional verification resolve different uncertainties, and each needs inputs that an early architectural description may not yet contain. Their cost includes preparing those inputs and interpreting failures as well as running the tools.

### Physical Constraints {#sec-physical-constraints-move-into-architecture}

A high-level model may predict throughput from array dimensions and memory capacity without knowing where the arrays and memories will be placed. Placement and routing determine the wire lengths, capacitances, and congestion that affect realized timing and energy [@KahngEtAl2011VLSIPhysicalDesign]. A larger cache can reduce misses while requiring longer wires and more leakage power, as in the opening example. Moving to a newer process node does not settle the trade-off, because logic cells, SRAM macros, and interconnects scale differently. The comparison needs the area, access time, and energy of the memory actually available in that process.

The cost of moving data explains why these physical details can reverse a ranking based on arithmetic alone. In the 45\ nm reference values compiled by @Horowitz2014Energy, SRAM and DRAM accesses consume much more energy than a local integer addition (@fig-data-movement-energy-scale). The access widths and memory capacities differ, so these values illustrate the importance of locality rather than supplying an energy model for a current chip.

```{python}
#| label: fig-data-movement-energy-scale
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Data movement can dominate arithmetic energy.** Reference $45\ \text{nm}$ energy values from @Horowitz2014Energy
#|   demonstrate a disparity of more than four orders of magnitude between local arithmetic (0.1\ pJ for a 32-bit integer add)
#|   and memory access (10–100\ pJ for on-chip static random-access memory (SRAM), 1.3–2.6\ nJ for off-chip DRAM, a $13{,}000\text{--}26{,}000\times$
#|   energy penalty). Architectural comparisons must represent data locality, buffer hierarchies, and memory
#|   traffic rather than counting arithmetic operations in isolation. Transcribed order-of-magnitude anchors,
#|   not current-node device estimates.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Log-scale plot comparing arithmetic and memory-access energy, showing a 32-bit integer add at 0.1 picojoules, static random-access memory (SRAM) accesses from 10 to 100 picojoules, and an off-chip DRAM access range from 1.3 to 2.6 nanojoules."

import csv
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style, draw_range_rows, row_axis, top_log_axis

# Source dataset: data/datasets/chapter2-horowitz-energy.csv (Horowitz, ISSCC 2014, 45 nm).
# Values are read from the CSV; ratios to the 32-bit integer add are computed here.
_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
with open(_root / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter2-horowitz-energy.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    src = [r for r in csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#"))]

baseline = float(src[0]["energy_low_pj"])


def _fmt_ratio(value):
    ratio = value / baseline
    return f"{ratio / 1000:.0f}k" if ratio >= 1000 and value >= 1000 else f"{ratio:.0f}"


rows = []
for r in src:
    low, high = float(r["energy_low_pj"]), float(r["energy_high_pj"])
    op, width = r["operation_or_access"], r["width_or_capacity"]
    if "SRAM" in op:
        capacity = width.replace(" 64 bit", "")
        label, note = f"{capacity} SRAM access", "64b access"
        color = COLORS["orange"] if high >= 100 else COLORS["green"]
    elif "DRAM" in op:
        label, note, color = "off-chip DRAM access", "64b access", COLORS["red"]
    else:
        label, note, color = f"{width.replace(' bit', 'b')} {op}", "local arithmetic", COLORS["blue"]
    right = f"{_fmt_ratio(low)}$\\times$" if low == high else f"{_fmt_ratio(low)}–{_fmt_ratio(high)}$\\times$"
    rows.append({"display_label": label, "display_note": note, "energy_low_pj": low,
                 "energy_high_pj": high, "right_label": right, "color": color})

apply_style()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.9, 3.2))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.40, right=0.80, top=0.82, bottom=0.08)

row_axis(ax, len(rows))
top_log_axis(
    ax,
    xlim=(0.06, 4000),
    xticks=[0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000],
    xticklabels=["0.1 pJ", "1 pJ", "10 pJ", "100 pJ", "1 nJ"],
    xlabel="rough energy per operation or access",
)
draw_range_rows(ax, rows, low_key="energy_low_pj", high_key="energy_high_pj", label_x=-0.82, right_x=1.04, label_fontsize=6.6, note_fontsize=5.4, right_fontsize=6.1, label_dy=-0.17, note_dy=0.23)

plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

The large separation between local arithmetic and memory access means that reducing an operation count can still increase energy if the new mapping sends more operands off chip. A system estimate must combine the workload's actual traffic with costs characterized for its implementation. The following decomposition keeps those contributions explicit:

$$
E_{\mathrm{system}} = E_{\mathrm{compute}} + E_{\mathrm{memory}} + E_{\mathrm{interconnect}} + E_{\mathrm{control}} + E_{\mathrm{leakage}}
$${#eq-system-energy-decomposition}

In @eq-system-energy-decomposition, a decrease in compute energy is beneficial only if it exceeds any increases in the other terms. The memory hierarchy matters through how often the workload reaches each level, just as the memory wall depends on access frequency and the latency the processor can hide [@WulfMcKee1995HittingMemoryWall]. Tile-to-tile traffic adds another cost. At runtime, overloaded links cause queueing and backpressure; during layout, the chosen network must fit within the available metal routing tracks. Runtime network congestion and physical routing congestion are distinct effects, although the floorplan can influence both.

Power delivery and heat removal add constraints that average energy cannot capture. When many execution units switch on together, a rapid current increase across the resistance and inductance of the supply network can lower the voltage reaching the cells. That transient droop may slow them enough to cause a timing failure. Sustained activity instead raises the question of whether the package can remove heat from where it is generated. In stacked designs, the position of active logic and the heat-removal path matter alongside total power. A thermal estimate therefore cannot establish that a rapid electrical transient is harmless.

Stronger checks need more information because they resolve those specific mechanisms. A timing analysis needs characterized cell delays, clock constraints, and wire estimates; a thermal analysis needs the placement of heat sources and package conditions. Timing must also be checked across specified operating modes and process, voltage, and temperature conditions [@Cadence2021Tempus]. A design that meets its cycle time under nominal conditions may fail under another required condition. Obtaining compatible libraries, memory macros, and package models is part of the evaluation cost even before the tools run.

Consider a floorplan search that ranks memory placements using a fast wirelength estimate. A compact placement may appear favorable yet crowd pins into a narrow routing channel. Detailed routing can then expose insufficient tracks, spacing violations, or delays that the proxy omitted. The failure does not automatically identify a bad architecture: the constraints or tool setup may also be wrong. Engineers must determine which explanation applies before deciding whether to repair the setup, revise the candidate, or broaden the search.

Multi-fidelity methods address this cost by combining inexpensive screening with selected evaluations that resolve consequential omissions [@PeherstorferWillcoxGunzburger2018Multifidelity]. More detailed analysis earns its cost when it answers a question that could change the decision. It does not replace the separate need to run representative workloads and establish correct behavior.

### Simulation Throughput and Fidelity

Detailed performance simulation exposes resource conflicts that simple models omit, but it executes much more slowly than native hardware. The 2013 zsim study reported detailed gem5, Flexus, and MARSS configurations running at about two hundred thousand target instructions per host second [@ZSim]. That historical rate is not a prediction for a current study; it shows why architects must measure their own simulator throughput before committing to workload lengths and candidate counts.

Faster execution often requires more setup or a different representation. Architectural simulators model selected timing interactions, compiled RTL simulators execute the circuit description, and field-programmable gate array (FPGA) platforms can accelerate longer runs. FireSim, for example, uses FPGA acceleration for full-system, cycle-exact RTL simulation [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. Preparing an FPGA model costs effort, and cycle-exact RTL execution still omits routed wire delays and package thermals. The choice depends on which behavior must be represented and how many runs can reuse the setup.

Sampling reduces runtime by selecting representative parts of a program. SimPoint selects program regions [@SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint], while SMARTS uses statistical sampling with explicit error bounds [@WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS]. The saving depends on how well those regions represent the workload and how caches and predictors are warmed before measurement. Analytical screening, sampled detailed simulation, and full-workload execution can therefore serve different stages of a comparison, with each retaining uncertainty that later work may need to resolve.

A coarse filter can discard a promising candidate or send an unsuitable one into an expensive run. Even a careful full-workload performance study, however, exercises only the behaviors reached by its inputs. It does not establish correctness across the legal state transitions that the design permits.

### Verification Bottlenecks

Verification is demanding because sequential storage creates a large space of possible states. A design with $n$ state bits can encode up to $2^n$ configurations. Reset and legal transitions restrict the reachable subset, but realistic processors and accelerators still have too many behaviors to check by brute-force enumeration. Changing a pipeline, cache protocol, or interface can introduce new interactions even when most of the implementation is reused.

Tests exercise selected behaviors under supplied inputs; a completed formal proof establishes a stated property for all behaviors covered by its model and assumptions [@Clarke2018ModelChecking]. When a proof is too difficult to complete, a bounded check can examine a limited number of cycles, but its conclusion stops at that bound. Functional coverage similarly reports which planned behaviors tests exercised, not the absence of every possible defect. Stronger claims therefore require broader checks, suitable assumptions, and enough time for the tools and engineers to complete them.

Verification effort belongs beside power, performance, and area (PPA) in an architectural comparison. A cache-coherence shortcut may improve simulated throughput yet introduce transient states and races whose verification exceeds the program's budget. The International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors (ITRS) Design chapter identified verification as a major bottleneck in 2001 [@ITRS2001Design], and the SRC MAPT roadmap continues to warn of a verification gap [@SemiconductorResearchCorporation2023MAPT]. This history motivates checking verification capacity; it does not establish that verification limits every project.

Industry staffing surveys show where effort has concentrated. The 2022 Wilson Research Group study of integrated circuit (IC) and ASIC projects reports verification staffing growing at about 6.2% per year from 2007 to 2022, compared with about 2.7% for design staffing [@Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy]. The indexed series in @fig-verification-demand-scissors distinguishes published data labels from chart-read approximations and tracks project staffing, rather than the marginal cost of checking one more candidate.

```{python}
#| label: fig-verification-demand-scissors
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Verification staffing grew faster than design staffing.** Mean peak staffing per IC/ASIC project
#|   indexed to a 2007 baseline demonstrates that verification engineer demand grew by 146% (a 6.2%
#|   compound annual growth rate [CAGR], reaching $\approx 2.46\times$) from 2007 to 2022, while design engineer demand grew by 50%
#|   (a 2.7% CAGR, reaching $\approx 1.50\times$) [@Foster2021WilsonPart8; @Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy]. Filled markers indicate
#|   printed data labels from published survey figures; hollow 2022 markers represent chart-read approximations
#|   constrained by the study's stated growth rates.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Two-line chart indexing engineer demand to 2007, with verification-engineer demand rising to about 2.5 times its 2007 level by 2022 while design-engineer demand reaches about 1.5 times, opening a widening gap between the lines."

import csv
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Mean peak engineers per IC/ASIC project, Wilson Research Group / Siemens EDA
# functional-verification studies (Foster's published summaries).
# Source data: data/datasets/chapter2-wilson-verification-staffing.csv. Rows with
# evidence_type == chart_read_constrained are drawn hollow; growth labels are computed.
_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
with open(_root / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter2-wilson-verification-staffing.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    staff = [r for r in csv.DictReader(fh) if r["year"].isdigit()]
years = [int(r["year"]) for r in staff]
design = [float(r["design_engineers_mean_peak"]) for r in staff]
verif = [float(r["verification_engineers_mean_peak"]) for r in staff]
printed = [r["evidence_type"] == "printed_data_label" for r in staff]

design_idx = [v / design[0] for v in design]
verif_idx = [v / verif[0] for v in verif]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.65, 2.3))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.12, right=0.80, top=0.93, bottom=0.19)

ax.plot(years, verif_idx, color=COLORS["green"], linewidth=1.6, zorder=2)
ax.plot(years, design_idx, color=COLORS["blue"], linewidth=1.6, zorder=2)
for x, v, d, solid in zip(years, verif_idx, design_idx, printed):
    if solid:
        ax.scatter([x], [v], s=22, color=COLORS["green"], zorder=3)
        ax.scatter([x], [d], s=20, marker="s", color=COLORS["blue"], zorder=3)
    else:
        ax.scatter([x], [v], s=26, facecolors="white", edgecolors=COLORS["green"], linewidths=1.1, zorder=3)
        ax.scatter([x], [d], s=24, marker="s", facecolors="white", edgecolors=COLORS["blue"], linewidths=1.1, zorder=3)

ax.text(years[-1] + 0.6, verif_idx[-1], f"verification\nengineers (+{(verif_idx[-1] - 1) * 100:.0f}%)",
        va="center", fontsize=6.0, color=COLORS["green"], clip_on=False)
ax.text(years[-1] + 0.6, design_idx[-1], f"design\nengineers (+{(design_idx[-1] - 1) * 100:.0f}%)",
        va="center", fontsize=6.0, color=COLORS["blue"], clip_on=False)

ax.set_xlim(years[0] - 1, years[-1] + 1)
ax.set_ylim(0.9, 2.7)
ax.set_xticks(years)
ax.set_yticks([1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5])
ax.set_yticklabels(["1.0$\\times$", "1.5$\\times$", "2.0$\\times$", "2.5$\\times$"])
ax.set_ylabel(f"mean peak demand vs. {years[0]}", fontsize=7)
ax.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=6.5, length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2)
ax.grid(axis="y", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.6)

for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)

plt.close(fig)
```

Faster growth in verification staffing does not identify a single cause, but it shows why generating more candidates cannot be assumed to reduce engineering effort. A candidate that reuses a familiar interface may retain much of its test and proof infrastructure; a changed interface can require new properties, stimulus, and failure analysis. The cost depends on what changed and what assurance the decision requires.

Some of that work concerns behavior absent from ordinary performance models. A signal crossing asynchronous clock domains can violate a receiving register's timing requirements and enter a metastable state, an analog condition that a cycle-level testbench does not represent. Suitable synchronizers or transfer protocols reduce that risk, while checks must also establish that the surrounding logical communication remains correct. Industry respin reports include clock-domain crossings, logic flaws, timing, and hardware–firmware interactions [@Foster2025WilsonVerification2024]. More random stimulus alone does not address every one of those mechanisms.

Escaped defects can require software workarounds that sacrifice performance or revised silicon. Intel's \$475M charge associated with the Pentium floating-point division defect illustrates the possible cost of a shipped arithmetic error [@Edelman1997PentiumDivision; @Intel1995PentiumCharge]. It does not establish a universal price for late defects, but it explains why teams spend substantial effort checking candidates before fabrication.

Generated hardware adds to this workload unless it arrives with usable, independently checked behavior. Published RTL-generation benchmarks report failures even at syntax parsing, interface compliance, and module-level functional testing [@VerilogEval; @RTLLM; @WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet]. A passing module test still leaves system integration and physical checks. Asking the same model to generate both the design and its tests can also reproduce the same misunderstanding in both, the correlated-failure problem illustrated by the Knight–Leveson experiment [@KnightLeveson1986Multiversion]. An independent reference or property that the generator cannot change is needed to expose such agreement on the wrong behavior.

The possible saving from a generated draft must therefore be compared with the work of integrating and checking it. Faster candidate creation helps when it removes missing implementation work; it can hinder progress when it consumes scarce verification capacity on additional failures. Physical implementation, software bring-up, and verification together determine how many alternatives a project can afford to develop.

\FloatBarrier

## The Economics of Specialized Silicon {#sec-design-cost-pressure}

Implementation, software, and verification consume a finite development budget. Much of this expense is non-recurring engineering (NRE), the upfront investment needed before volume production. Its scale influences both the architecture a program can justify and the number of alternatives it can develop far enough to compare.

Public estimates illustrate the investment without establishing a universal project price (@fig-design-cost-by-node). A 2018 International Business Strategies (IBS) series estimated IC design costs of \$51.3M at 28\ nm, \$297.8M at 7\ nm, and \$542.2M at 5\ nm [@LaPedus2018BigTrouble3nm]. Arm's 2023 prospectus cites a July 2022 IBS series estimating \$249M at 7\ nm and \$725M at 2\ nm [@ArmHoldings2023Prospectus]. The differing estimates at the same node show why these figures must retain their vintages and assumptions about reuse and design scope. Both series nevertheless place a substantial development investment behind leading-node specialization.

```{python}
#| label: fig-design-cost-by-node
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Leading-node design-cost estimates rise steeply, and they depend on the estimate's vintage.** Each bar is an
#|   International Business Strategies (IBS) estimate, labeled with the year of the IBS series it comes from
#|   [@LaPedus2018BigTrouble3nm; @ArmHoldings2023Prospectus]. The two vintages differ at 7\ nm (\$298M versus \$249M),
#|   so the bars are published estimates under different assumptions, not a controlled node-scaling series or universal project prices.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bar chart of IC design-cost estimates by process node. The 2018 estimates are 51 million dollars at 28 nanometers, 298 million at 7 nanometers, and 542 million at 5 nanometers. The 2022 estimates, drawn hatched, are 249 million at 7 nanometers and 725 million at 2 nanometers."

import csv
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
```

That investment extends well beyond writing RTL. In the 2\ nm estimate cited by Arm, software development, verification, and IP qualification together account for 71% of the total [@ArmHoldings2023Prospectus]. The split describes one cost model, not the critical path of every program, but it makes a useful distinction: accelerating a local drafting task does not eliminate the surrounding work needed to ship the design. Assistance that creates more integration or verification work may move expense rather than reduce it.

Production volume determines how heavily development cost weighs on each shipped chip. In a simple accounting model,

$$
C_{\mathrm{unit}} = C_{\mathrm{variable}} + \frac{C_{\mathrm{NRE}}}{V},
$$

where $C_{\mathrm{variable}}$ is average manufacturing, packaging, and test cost per unit, $C_{\mathrm{NRE}}$ is allocated development investment, and $V$ is shipment volume. The model omits financing and time-to-market effects, but it explains why the same specialized design can be attractive at one volume and difficult to justify at another. Reusing qualified IP or a chiplet across products can spread the investment, while programmable engines retain flexibility at an area or energy cost.

For a mobile-XR program, the decision is whether custom silicon's efficiency and capability gains justify the hardware, software, and verification work at the anticipated volume. Retaining an existing processor, reusing more IP, or choosing a less expensive process may improve the economic balance while giving up performance or energy efficiency. These are architecture alternatives, not merely accounting adjustments after the design is chosen.

Evaluation itself consumes part of that finite budget. A detailed simulation or integration test can justify its expense when it resolves an uncertainty that would otherwise lead to costly redesign. More candidate generation is useful when it creates better options worth evaluating. Neither investment pays automatically; its value depends on the decision it improves and the total resources required to reach it.

## Locating the Bottleneck and Choosing Assistance {#sec-compounding-design-loop-pressure}

A design study encounters these pressures together. A different memory organization may need new compiler support, which changes traffic and the physical power comparison. One candidate may reuse existing tests, while another needs new properties and integration checks. The effort required to learn from an alternative depends on the work downstream of the proposal, so accelerating one step can expose a slower one elsewhere.

### Diagnosing the Work That Limits Progress

The limiting work is visible in a project's unfinished decisions. A team may be waiting for a workload trace, a characterized memory macro, an executable compiler path, or a verification engineer to diagnose a failure. Queue ages and lengths reveal where work accumulates; repeated runs reveal time lost to changed inputs or mistaken configurations. Industry trends help explain why these pressures arise, but only the program's own work can establish which one currently matters.

The MAESTRO example in @tbl-design-loop-scale-anchors shows why a fast optimizer may have little value when the work around it is incomplete. Its analytical model can score many mappings cheaply, yet changed layer shapes can make the winner irrelevant to deployment, and physical or verification checks may reject it later. Improving workload inputs or checking selected candidates can help more than accelerating an already inexpensive analytical step.

Likewise, a simulator run against an outdated workload or misconfigured memory model occupies a compute slot without answering the architecture question. Correcting those inputs increases useful evaluation throughput even when the simulator runs no faster. In another project, the inputs may be sound but every candidate allowed by the hardware template may miss the target. More runs then cannot supply a feasible design; the architect has to reconsider the organization or the requirements.

When viable proposals are flowing, evaluation and review capacity limit how much work can finish. A backlog grows at a stage whenever more work enters than completes over the same interval (@fig-scissors-gap). Candidate counts alone hide this imbalance because some candidates pass a quick check while others require long simulations or new verification effort.

<!-- arch2-allow: figure-placement-override The print-size workflow needs flexible placement beside the conditional backlog discussion. -->

Waiting work grows at a stage when admissions exceed completions over the same interval; candidate counts must be interpreted alongside the different checking costs they impose.
